Today's pages (pp. 51–56) show Percy's ordinary life ending. Pairing them with a Raven story from Alaska shows that stories from different cultures use crossings and transformations to show what a community values.","enduringUnderstanding":"Stories from different traditions use heroes who cross boundaries and change worlds to express shared values such as sacrifice, change, and responsibility.","futureLessons":"Lesson 12 (Chapter 5, pp. 57–66) follows Percy into Camp Half-Blood, where themes of grief, identity, and belonging begin to emerge. Today's habits of citing evidence and comparing texts carry forward into later paragraphs and discussions.","performanceTask":"Shared Stories, Shared Lessons asks students to explain how two texts show a transition or transformation. Today's comparative paragraph is a first practice of that skill: cross-text evidence, central ideas, and a formal, cohesive explanation."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"transform","definition":"to change something completely in form, nature, or appearance","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"sacrifice","definition":"giving up something important for the sake of someone or something else","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"boundary","definition":"a line or limit that separates one place or state from another","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"responsibility","definition":"a duty to take care of someone or something","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"formal style","definition":"serious, precise school writing that avoids slang, contractions, and 'you'","tier":"support"},{"word":"evidence","definition":"details from a text that support an idea","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Book 1)","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Chapter 4, pp. 51–56"},{"title":"Myths and Legends of Alaska: a Raven creation tale in which Raven brings daylight","author":"Katharine B. Judson (collector)","pages":"Raven story selected by the teacher (about 1–2 pages)"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Spark thinking about moments when a character's world changes and connect to today's comparison of Percy and Raven.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"When Your World Changes","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.3"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"TEXT SELECTION: The Outline asks you to choose one specific Raven story from Katharine B. Judson's Myths and Legends of Alaska (public domain). This Lesson assumes a tale in which Raven brings daylight to a dark world. Before class, find that tale in the Judson text, print it (about 1–2 pages), and check the details against the sample responses below. If your version differs, adjust the sample responses and the Raven evidence to match the printed copy."},{"type":"directions","text":"Think of a moment in a story, movie, or your own life when everything changed and there was no going back. Turn to a partner and describe it in one or two sentences."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does it feel like when a character crosses from an old world into a new one?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It feels scary but also exciting, because the character can't go back to normal. Like in a movie when someone leaves home and has to figure out a brand-new place."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today you will read about two crossings. Percy crosses toward the lights of a farmhouse at the end of Chapter 4. Raven brings change from darkness into a new world. You will write a short, formal paragraph comparing them."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Review transitions, precise language, and formal style in explanatory writing using a teacher-written mentor paragraph.","activities":[{"id":"lab-mentor-sentences","title":"Transitions, Precise Language, and Formal Style","minutes":6,"standards":["W.6.2.c","W.6.2.d","W.6.2.e"],"routine":"Language Study","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Strong explanatory writers do three things. They use transitions to show how ideas relate, such as similarly, in contrast, as a result, and in both stories. They choose precise words, such as confronts instead of meets, or vanishes instead of goes away. And they keep a formal style: no slang, no contractions, no 'you,' and no 'I think.'"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read the mentor sentences below. With a partner, underline the transitions, circle the precise words, and find one thing that makes the style formal."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Mentor sentences (teacher-written): *After Percy defeats the Minotaur and loses his mother, he carries Grover toward the farmhouse lights, and this crossing ends his ordinary life. Similarly, Raven releases daylight into a world of darkness; as a result, the world is permanently transformed.*"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which words show how the ideas connect, and what do they tell the reader?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"After, and this crossing ends, show the order and result for Percy. Similarly shows the two stories are alike, and as a result shows that Raven's action caused the change."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which words are precise, and how is the style formal?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Defeats, carries, releases, and permanently transformed are precise. It is formal because it has no contractions, no 'I' or 'you,' and it states facts about the texts."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students notice how transitions and precise verbs make explanations clearer and more formal (ELD.PI.6.7).","sayAsk":"Say: Read the mentor sentences aloud with me. Point to the transition. Ask: Which word tells us the stories are alike? Which verb is stronger than 'goes'? Frames: Similarly, ___. As a result, ___. Percy ___ (confronts / carries / crosses) ___. Offer an everyday-to-formal upgrade: You said Percy ran away; we can say Percy crossed toward the farmhouse.","watchFor":"If students use only 'and then,' then prompt: Which transition shows a result? A comparison? If students use slang or contractions, then prompt: Say it again in formal school language. Success: the student names a transition and explains what relationship it shows."}]},{"id":"lab-expand-sentences","title":"Adding Details with Adverbials","minutes":4,"standards":["W.6.2.d","L.6.1","L.6.3"],"routine":"Sentence Expansion","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Adverbials tell when, where, how, or why. Watch me expand a plain sentence: Percy crosses. Next: Percy crosses toward the farmhouse lights. Next: Reluctantly, because his mother has vanished, Percy crosses toward the farmhouse lights."},{"type":"directions","text":"With a partner, expand this sentence in two steps: *Raven changes the world.* Add one detail about how or when, and one detail about why or where."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details did you add, and what did they show the reader?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Cleverly, Raven changes the world by freeing the daylight that had been hidden in the dark. Cleverly shows how, and by freeing the daylight shows what caused the change."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Build the ability to expand sentences with adverbials of time, place, manner, and cause (ELD.PII.6.5).","sayAsk":"Say: Let's build a sentence one layer at a time. Ask: When? Where? How? Why? Frames: ___ (adverb), ___ crosses ___. After ___, Percy ___. Raven acts ___ because ___. Emerging students add one prepositional phrase; Expanding students add two kinds; Bridging students add a clause.","watchFor":"If students add details that are not in the text, then prompt: Where does the text show that? If students string many phrases together, then prompt: Which two details matter most? Success: the student expands a sentence with at least one accurate adverbial."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: choosing transitions","tryThis":"Give a short transition bank sorted by purpose: order (after, then, finally), comparison (similarly, in both stories), contrast (however, in contrast), result (as a result, therefore). Have students label each mentor transition by purpose."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to rewrite the mentor sentences with a different transition and explain how the meaning shifts, or to replace each general verb with a more connotative one."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students gather evidence from Chapter 4 and the Raven story (W.6.9) and analyze the crossings and central ideas. Part B: Students draft a formal comparative paragraph with transitions and precise language (W.6.2.c, W.6.2.d, W.6.2.e).","activities":[{"id":"lia-gather-evidence","title":"Part A: Gather Evidence from Both Texts","minutes":10,"standards":["W.6.9","RL.6.1","RL.6.3"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 4","pages":"pp. 51–56"},{"type":"text-reference","title":"Raven creation tale from Myths and Legends of Alaska (teacher-selected)","pages":"Full tale"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 51–56 and the Raven story. Make a three-column chart: Text, Key action or description, What it shows about change. Record at least two pieces of evidence for Percy (the fight with the Minotaur, his mother's disappearance, the crossing toward the farmhouse lights) and at least two for Raven (such as Raven bringing light or reshaping the land). Paraphrase or use short quotations."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do the Minotaur fight, the loss of his mother, and the farmhouse lights show that Percy's life is turning a corner?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy fights a monster he thought was only a myth, then his mother vanishes in front of him, and then he carries Grover toward the lights of a safe place. His old life is gone, and he can only move forward into a new one. That makes this section a turning point."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Raven do in the story, and how does that change the world?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Raven gets the light that was kept hidden and lets it out. Before, the world was dark. After, people can see and live in a new way. Raven's cleverness changes everything for humans."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate and check that each piece of evidence names a specific action, not a general feeling. Push students toward 'what happened, and what changed because of it.' Check Raven evidence against the printed copy you selected."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1","W.6.9"],"stem":"Which piece of evidence from Chapter 4 best shows that this section is a turning point for Percy?","choices":[{"text":"Percy defeats the Minotaur, his mother disappears, and he carries Grover toward the farmhouse lights, leaving his old life behind.","correct":true,"rationale":"This names specific events from pp. 51–56 and explains how together they end his ordinary life and move him toward a new world."},{"text":"Percy is tired and thinks the storm is very loud.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is a believable detail about the scene, but it does not show a change in Percy's journey."},{"text":"Grover is nervous throughout the whole chapter.","correct":false,"rationale":"Grover's panic matters in earlier pages, but it does not explain why this section is a turning point for Percy."},{"text":"Percy likes his school and wants to go back.","correct":false,"rationale":"This misreads the section; Percy cannot go back, and the text points him forward toward the camp."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in selecting and explaining text evidence with precise language (ELD.PI.6.7, ELD.PI.6.10).","sayAsk":"Say: Point to the sentence that shows the change. Ask: What action happens? What changes because of it? Frames: In Chapter 4, Percy ___. This shows that ___. In the Raven story, Raven ___, so the world ___. Offer a word bank: confronts, vanishes, crosses, releases, transforms.","watchFor":"If students retell the whole chapter, then prompt: Which one action shows the turning point? If students cite only Percy, then prompt: What is the evidence for Raven? Success: the student pairs one action with a clear explanation of change for each text."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding evidence","tryThis":"Give page ranges and a focus question for each column. Pre-mark one passage in each text and have students find the action verbs."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to find a word or phrase in each text with strong connotation (such as light, dark, or vanish) and explain its impact on tone."}]}]},{"id":"lia-analyze-crossing","title":"Part A: Analyze the Crossing and Shared Values","minutes":8,"standards":["RL.6.2","RL.6.9","W.6.9"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"With a partner, use your chart to answer: What boundary does each character cross? What new world is created? Which central idea (sacrifice, change, or responsibility) do both texts share? Add a fourth column labeled Central idea."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Percy leave behind, and what does Raven leave behind?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy leaves his old life with his mother and his belief that monsters are not real. Raven leaves behind a world of darkness, so the old state of the world ends."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What shared value do these transformations reflect?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Both show responsibility and sacrifice. Percy loses his mother and still protects Grover. Raven risks himself to give light to others. Change costs something, but it helps someone else."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Accept sacrifice, change, or responsibility as long as students support it with evidence from both texts. Remind students that the stories come from different traditions, so a shared value is a similarity in what the stories teach, not a claim that they are the same story."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students compare two texts orally with precise language before writing (ELD.PI.6.7).","sayAsk":"Say: Tell your partner how the stories are alike and different. Ask: Who crosses a boundary? What is the new world? Frames: Both Percy and Raven ___. Percy ___, whereas Raven ___. Both stories show that ___ requires ___.","watchFor":"If students list differences only, then prompt: What do both characters give up or risk? If students make claims without evidence, then prompt: Which action shows that? Success: the student states one similarity and supports it with an action from each text."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding a shared idea","tryThis":"Offer three choices (sacrifice, change, responsibility) and ask: What does each character give up or protect? Which word fits both?"},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain one important difference between the two crossings (a world changed for many versus a personal journey) and how it affects the message."}]}]},{"id":"lia-draft-paragraph","title":"Part B: Draft the Comparative Paragraph","minutes":12,"standards":["W.6.2.c","W.6.2.d","W.6.2.e","W.6.9","W.6.4","W.6.5"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Let me model. My topic sentence names both characters and the big idea: Percy Jackson and Raven each act as world-changers who cross a boundary at a cost. Then I give evidence for Percy, evidence for Raven, a transition that connects them, and a closing sentence that names the new world each creates. I check for formal style and underline my transitions."},{"type":"directions","text":"Write one paragraph (6–8 sentences) that answers: How do Percy and Raven each act as a boundary-crosser or world-changer, and what new world or reality do their actions create? Include: a topic sentence naming both characters; at least one piece of evidence from each text (Percy, Chapter 4, pp. 51–56; Raven, the selected tale); at least three different transitions, underlined; precise words and at least one expanded sentence with an adverbial; a formal style (no contractions, slang, or 'I' or 'you'); and a closing sentence about what new world their actions create and what value it reflects."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Sample paragraph: Percy Jackson and Raven each act as world-changers who cross a boundary at a great cost. In Chapter 4, Percy defeats the Minotaur, watches his mother vanish, and then carries Grover toward the farmhouse lights, which ends his ordinary life. As a result, he enters a world of gods and monsters he never knew existed. Similarly, Raven brings light into a world of darkness, and this action permanently transforms life for humans. Although Percy acts to survive and Raven acts out of cleverness, both give up the old, familiar world so a new one can begin. Both stories therefore suggest that change requires sacrifice and that heroes accept responsibility for others."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which sentence in your paragraph shows how the two stories connect, and which transition makes that connection clear?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My sentence that begins with Similarly connects the stories. It shows that Raven also changes the world, just like Percy's crossing changes his life."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Confer first with students who write two separate summaries. Ask: Where is the comparison? Remind students that evidence should be paraphrased or briefly quoted, with the explanation in their own words."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Checklist: Does my topic sentence name both characters and the shared idea? Do I have evidence from both texts? Do I use at least three different transitions? Are my words precise? Is my style formal? Does my last sentence name the new world and the value?"},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in writing a formal comparative paragraph using adverbials, transitions, and precise language (ELD.PI.6.10, ELD.PII.6.5).","sayAsk":"Say: Say your first sentence to a partner before you write it. Ask: What does each character do? What changes? Frames: Percy and Raven both ___. In Chapter 4, Percy ___; as a result, ___. Similarly, Raven ___ so that ___. Both stories show that ___. Offer everyday-to-formal upgrades: You said the world got different; we can say the world was permanently transformed.","watchFor":"If students copy from the text, then prompt: Close the book and say it in your own words. If students use informal language, then prompt: Replace the slang with precise, formal wording. If the paragraph lacks Raven evidence, then prompt: What does Raven do that changes the world? Success: the student writes a paragraph with evidence from both texts, varied transitions, and formal style."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: organizing the paragraph","tryThis":"Provide a frame: Percy and Raven each ___. In Chapter 4, Percy ___. As a result, ___. Similarly, Raven ___. Therefore, ___. Allow students to rehearse each sentence aloud first."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Challenge students to add a sentence analyzing how one precise word (such as vanish or release) shapes the meaning, or to revise a simple transition into a more sophisticated one."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Reflect on how transitions, evidence, and formal style helped explain a transformation, a skill needed for the Performance Task.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-turn-and-talk","title":"Why Compare Two Worlds?","minutes":5,"standards":["W.6.2.c","W.6.9"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Share your paragraph's topic sentence with a partner. Then discuss: How did using evidence from both texts, and transitions between them, help you explain the transformation?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why is it important to use evidence from both texts when you compare them?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Evidence from both shows the comparison is real, not just my opinion. Transitions like similarly help the reader see how Percy's crossing and Raven's change connect."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In the Performance Task, you will explain how two texts show a transformation. Today you practiced the core move: evidence, connection, and a clear, formal explanation."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (Optional)","purpose":"Prepare for Lesson 12 by reading the next chapter.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-ch5","title":"Read and Annotate Chapter 5","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.10"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 5","pages":"pp. 57–66"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read and annotate Chapter 5. Mark places where Percy's new surroundings, feelings, or choices show him entering a new world."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students gathered evidence from The Lightning Thief Chapter 4 (pp. 51–56) and a teacher-selected Raven world-shaping tale from Judson's Myths and Legends of Alaska to explain how Percy and Raven cross boundaries and change worlds. They then wrote a formal comparative paragraph using transitions, precise language, and cross-text evidence to name shared ideas of sacrifice, change, and responsibility.","keyActivities":["Mentor-sentence study of transitions, precise language, and formal style","Adverbial sentence expansion","Evidence chart for Chapter 4 and the Raven tale","Partner analysis of crossings and shared values","Quick Write comparative paragraph with checklist"],"vocabularyTaught":["transform","sacrifice","boundary","responsibility","formal style","evidence"],"standardsCovered":["W.6.2.c","W.6.2.d","W.6.2.e","W.6.9","RL.6.1","RL.6.2","RL.6.3","RL.6.9","W.6.4","W.6.5","L.6.1","L.6.3","RL.6.10","ELD.PI.6.10","ELD.PI.6.7","ELD.PII.6.5"]}}
